config.title: Utility Types — Built-in Transformers

intro.title: Utility Types — Built-in Transformers
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple user profile system using TypeScript's built-in utility types to transform and manipulate object types. You'll learn how to use key utility types like `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, and `Pick` to create flexible and type-safe data structures. The core concept is leveraging these transformers to modify existing types without rewriting them, ensuring your code is both efficient and robust. By the end, you'll understand how to apply these utilities to manage optional fields, enforce required properties, and extract subsets of types in your TypeScript projects.
intro.usecase: Utility types are essential for managing complex data shapes in real-world applications, such as admin dashboards where you need to display partial user data in a table while requiring full details for editing in a modal. For example, when building a user management panel, you might use `Pick` to create a type for a read-only summary view and `Omit` to exclude sensitive fields like passwords before sending data to the client. In a dynamic form builder, `Partial` can be used to handle incremental validation states, and `Required` ensures all fields are filled before submission. These built-in transformers help developers enforce type safety, reduce bugs, and streamline API interactions in products like e-commerce platforms or content management systems.

objectives: Construct new types by applying the `Partial` utility to make all properties optional
Implement the `Readonly` utility to prevent modification of object properties
Manipulate existing types using the `Pick` utility to extract specific properties
Configure the `Omit` utility to create types by excluding specified properties
Initialize the `Record` utility to define objects with specified key-value types
Apply the `Required` utility to enforce that all optional properties become mandatory
Integrate multiple utility types to transform complex type definitions

steps.title: Import TypeScript utilities and define base types
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript file and define a base interface called 'User' with properties: id (number), name (string), email (string), and active (boolean).
steps.hint: Start by writing an interface declaration with the required properties and their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface is created with the correct property types, ready for utility type transformations.
successCriteria: The User interface is defined with id: number, name: string, email: string, and active: boolean properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that all four properties (id, name, email, active) are present with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface is missing or has incorrect properties. Review the required properties: id (number), name (string), email (string), active (boolean).

steps.title: Implement Partial<T> to make all properties optional
steps.instruction: Create a new type named 'PartialUser' that applies the Partial<T> utility to the existing 'User' interface, making all properties optional.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: type PartialUser = Partial<User>;
steps.seedCode:
// Define your User interface here

// Create PartialUser type here
steps.expectedOutcome: A new type PartialUser is created where all properties from User are optional.
successCriteria: PartialUser type is defined using Partial<User>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the Partial utility correctly with the User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PartialUser type wasn't created correctly. Remember to use Partial<User> to make all properties optional.

steps.title: Implement Required<T> to make all properties mandatory
steps.instruction: Create a new type named RequiredUser using the Required<T> utility type, based on the existing User interface.
steps.hint: Use the syntax 'type RequiredUser = Required<User>;' to create a type where all properties from User become required.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new RequiredUser type is created using the Required<T> utility type.
successCriteria: RequiredUser type is defined using Required<User>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the Required<T> utility type with the User interface to create the RequiredUser type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The RequiredUser type wasn't created correctly. Remember to use the Required<T> utility type with the User interface.

steps.title: Implement Readonly<T> to make properties immutable
steps.instruction: Create a new type named ReadonlyUser by applying the Readonly<T> utility type to your User interface.
steps.hint: Use the syntax 'type ReadonlyUser = Readonly<User>;' to create a type where all properties from User become readonly.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: making an object type immutable
type ImmutablePoint = Readonly<{ x: number; y: number }>;
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a ReadonlyUser type that prevents property reassignment, enforcing immutability.
successCriteria: The ReadonlyUser type is defined using Readonly<User>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the Readonly utility type with your User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Try creating a type named ReadonlyUser that applies Readonly<T> to the User interface.

steps.title: Implement Pick<T, K> to select specific properties
steps.instruction: Create a new type named 'PickUser' using the Pick utility type to select only the 'name' and 'email' properties from the User interface.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: type PickUser = Pick<User, 'property1' | 'property2'>. Remember to include the union of property names as the second type parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new type 'PickUser' is defined using the Pick utility type, containing only the 'name' and 'email' properties from the User interface.
successCriteria: The PickUser type is correctly defined with Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct syntax: Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The PickUser type isn't defined correctly. Remember to use Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> to select only those properties.

steps.title: Implement Omit<T, K> to exclude specific properties
steps.instruction: Create a new type named OmitUser that uses the Omit utility type to exclude the 'email' and 'age' properties from the User interface.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: type OmitUser = Omit<User, 'property1' | 'property2'>
steps.expectedOutcome: A new OmitUser type is defined that contains all User properties except 'email' and 'age'.
successCriteria: OmitUser type is created using Omit<User, 'email' | 'age'>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the Omit utility type with the correct syntax and excluding both 'email' and 'age'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The OmitUser type wasn't created correctly. Check the syntax: type OmitUser = Omit<User, 'email' | 'age'>

steps.title: Implement Record<K, T> to create mapped object types
steps.instruction: Create a new type named UserRoles using Record<K, T> that maps user IDs (as strings) to role names (as strings).
steps.hint: Use the syntax: type UserRoles = Record<string, string>;
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: mapping product IDs to product names
type ProductCatalog = Record<string, string>;
steps.expectedOutcome: A UserRoles type is defined using Record<string, string> to create a mapped object type.
successCriteria: UserRoles type is created with Record<string, string> syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the Record<K, T> utility type with string for both key and value types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The UserRoles type should be created using Record<string, string>. Review the Record<K, T> syntax for creating mapped object types.

steps.title: Implement Exclude<T, U> to exclude union types
steps.instruction: Create a type named ExcludedUserRole using Exclude<T, U> that excludes 'admin' from the UserRole union type.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: type ExcludedUserRole = Exclude<UserRole, 'admin'>;
steps.expectedOutcome: A new type ExcludedUserRole is defined using Exclude to remove 'admin' from the UserRole union.
successCriteria: The ExcludedUserRole type is correctly defined using Exclude<UserRole, 'admin'>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but ensure you're using the correct syntax: type ExcludedUserRole = Exclude<UserRole, 'admin'>;
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax for Exclude<T, U>. It should be: type ExcludedUserRole = Exclude<UserRole, 'admin'>;

steps.title: Implement Extract<T, U> to extract union types
steps.instruction: Create a type named ExtractedUserRole using Extract<T, U> that extracts only the 'admin' and 'editor' roles from the UserRole union type.
steps.hint: Use Extract<UserRole, 'admin' | 'editor'> to create a type that includes only those specific union members.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new type ExtractedUserRole is defined using Extract to filter the UserRole union to only include 'admin' and 'editor'.
successCriteria: ExtractedUserRole type is created with Extract<UserRole, 'admin' | 'editor'> syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using Extract with the correct union types and extracted members.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ExtractedUserRole type isn't correctly implemented. Remember to use Extract<UserRole, 'admin' | 'editor'>.

steps.title: Create demonstration function to showcase all utility types
steps.instruction: Create a function named demonstrateUtilityTypes that returns a string demonstrating the usage of all the utility types you've implemented.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses each of your custom types (PartialUser, RequiredUser, etc.) and returns a descriptive string.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that consolidates all the utility type implementations into a single demonstration.
successCriteria: The demonstrateUtilityTypes function is defined and returns a string that references all the implemented utility types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it references all the utility types (PartialUser, RequiredUser, ReadonlyUser, PickUser, OmitUser, UserRoles, ExcludedUserRole, ExtractedUserRole) in its implementation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't properly demonstrate the utility types. Review the previous steps to ensure you're using all the types you created.
